title: The European Parliament Just Condemned Pakistan for the Forced Conversion of Hindu and Christian Girls. The Numbers Are Staggering.
excerpt: Seventy-five per cent of forced conversion victims in Pakistan are Hindu. The EU resolution calls out a court ruling that validated the marriage of a 13-year-old Christian girl to her 30-year-old abductor.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • 75% of forced conversion victims in Pakistan are Hindu, highlighting a severe crisis.
  • The EU condemned Pakistan for endorsing child marriage and forced conversions of minority girls.
  • Maria Shahbaz's case exemplifies broader human rights violations against minorities in Pakistan.
  • UN rapporteurs demand an end to forced conversions, emphasizing the need for consent.
  • The EU resolution strengthens India's advocacy for the rights of Hindu minorities in Pakistan.
The Scale of Forced Conversions
75%
Hindu Victims of Forced Conversion
25%
Christian Victims of Forced Conversion
80%
Incidents in Sindh Province
14-18
Age Range of Most Affected Girls
Younger
Some Victims Reportedly Younger
Based on 2025 UN figures
The European Parliament has adopted a resolution condemning Pakistan for the abduction, forced conversion, and child marriage of girls from Hindu and Christian minorities — the most forceful intervention yet by a Western legislative body on a crisis that has drawn outrage from India and the diaspora worldwide. The resolution, passed this week, singled out the case of Maria Shahbaz, a 13-year-old Christian girl from Lahore who was abducted in July 2025, forcibly converted to Islam, and married to her 30-year-old abductor. Pakistan's Federal Constitutional Court upheld the marriage in March 2026, citing sharia law — a ruling that effectively overrode the country's own Child Marriage Restraint Act. ## The Scale of the Crisis The EU resolution cited 2025 United Nations figures that lay bare the religious dimensions of the crisis: among women and girls affected by forced conversion through marriage in Pakistan, approximately 75 per cent were Hindu and 25 per cent were Christian. Nearly 80 per cent of incidents were recorded in Sindh Province. Adolescent girls between 14 and 18 were identified as particularly vulnerable, though some victims were reportedly younger. The European Parliament urged Pakistan's authorities to "fully implement the country's national framework to end child marriage" and to "create a national mechanism for handling complaints from families of abducted or forcibly converted girls from minorities." Members of the European Parliament stressed that Maria Shahbaz's case was "emblematic of broader human rights violations faced by minorities in Pakistan" and called for her to have access to legal representation, her family, and psychological support. ![Sindh Province — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d1/Jinnah_Mausoleum.JPG/3840px-Jinnah_Mausoleum.JPG) > **""These women and girls endure a continuous sense of terror, face coercion and are deprived of their freedom of religion or belief and autonomy under patriarchal and political pressures."** ## A Court Ruling That Sparked Global Backlash The crisis escalated dramatically after Pakistan's Federal Constitutional Court validated Maria's forced marriage on March 25, 2026. The ruling drew swift condemnation from human rights organisations, Church leaders, and Pakistani civil society. Archbishop Khalid Rehmat of Lahore, head of Pakistan's largest Catholic diocese, called the decision "profoundly disturbing" and "unacceptable," warning that it "sends a dangerous message that undermines the rule of law and weakens protections for vulnerable minority girls across the country." Peter Jacob, executive director of the Centre for Social Justice in Pakistan, pointed out that the court's reliance on sharia superseded multiple federal and provincial laws — including the Punjab Child Marriage Restraint Ordinance 2026, the Sindh Child Marriage Restraint Act 2013, and the Balochistan Child Marriage Restraint Act 2025 — all of which set the minimum marriage age for girls at 18. The Pakistani government has responded by quietly forming a 37-member national committee, including Catholic and Protestant bishops, to review the case and propose safeguards against forced conversions and marriages. A formal announcement has not yet been made. ## The UN Joins the Pressure Separately, a panel of UN special rapporteurs issued an unusually pointed statement calling on Pakistan to end forced conversions and marriages of minority women and girls. The panel included rapporteurs on slavery, religious freedom, minority rights, trafficking, and violence against women. "These women and girls endure a continuous sense of terror, face coercion and are deprived of their freedom of religion or belief and autonomy under patriarchal and political pressures. This must stop," the panel stated. ![Federal Constitutional Court — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5b/Geb%C3%A4udekomplex_des_Bundesverfassungsgerichts_%28Baumgarten-Bau%29_-_Bauteil_III_5.jpg/3840px-Geb%C3%A4udekomplex_des_Bundesverfassungsgerichts_%28Baumgarten-Bau%29_-_Bauteil_III_5.jpg)
Legal and Social Backlash
›March 25, 2026 Court ruling validated forced marriage of a 13-year-old.
›Archbishop calls ruling 'profoundly disturbing'.
›Multiple laws set minimum marriage age at 18.
›Pakistan forms a 37-member committee to review the case.
The rapporteurs warned that impunity was enabling the practice to persist and that conversions carried out through marriage "must be free from coercion and based on full and free consent — conditions that cannot be met when the victim is a child." ## Why This Matters to the Indian Diaspora The resolution carries particular weight for the Indian diaspora and for India's relationship with Pakistan. The fact that 75 per cent of forced conversion victims are Hindu — members of Pakistan's most marginalised religious minority — has made this a deeply emotional issue for Hindu communities worldwide. India has long raised the plight of Hindu minorities in Pakistan at international forums. The EU resolution reinforces New Delhi's position and adds significant Western institutional backing to the campaign for minority rights protection in Pakistan. For NRIs, particularly those with roots in Sindh — where the overwhelming majority of forced conversions occur, and which was home to a large Hindu population before Partition — the resolution touches on questions of ancestral heritage, religious freedom, and the safety of communities that remained in Pakistan. The EU resolution also implicitly undermines Pakistan's diplomatic narrative. Islamabad has invested heavily in projecting religious tolerance through initiatives like the Kartarpur Corridor and the facilitation of Sikh pilgrimages. The European Parliament's formal condemnation challenges that image with documented evidence of systemic abuse. ## What Comes Next
International Pressure Mounts
›UN rapporteurs demand an end to forced conversions.
›Victims face coercion and lack of autonomy.
›EU resolution reinforces India's advocacy for minority rights.
›Calls for linking trade concessions to minority rights progress.
The resolution is non-binding, and Pakistan has historically resisted external pressure on its treatment of minorities. But the convergence of EU parliamentary action, UN rapporteur intervention, and domestic judicial controversy creates a level of international scrutiny that Islamabad will find difficult to deflect. Human rights organisations are calling for the EU to link its Generalised Scheme of Preferences (GSP+) trade concessions — which Pakistan benefits from — to measurable progress on minority rights. That would give the resolution real economic teeth.
